nameStory: Jasmine tobacco gets its name from its sweetly fragrant white flowers that bloom at night, releasing a perfume similar to jasmine. The word 'tobacco' comes from the Spanish 'tabaco,' though this ornamental species is grown for beauty rather than smoking. Some also call it 'winged tobacco' because of the way its leaves extend down the stem like little wings.
description: Jasmine tobacco is a tall annual flower that can reach 3-5 feet high, originally from South America but grown as a garden ornamental. It produces clusters of trumpet-shaped white or pale pink flowers that open in the evening and release an intoxicating sweet fragrance. The plant has large, soft green leaves and a sturdy upright stem. While it's in the same family as tomatoes and potatoes, this tobacco relative is purely decorative in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long white trumpet-shaped flowers about 3-4 inches long that open at dusk and release an incredibly sweet, jasmine-like fragrance that can be detected from many feet away

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, soft, sticky leaves that feel somewhat fuzzy to the touch and have a slightly sweet, tobacco-like smell when crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall upright annual plant reaching 3-5 feet with a single main stem and branching flower clusters at the top

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small oval seed capsules that split open to release tiny brown seeds, developing after the tubular flowers fade

habitat: In New England, jasmine tobacco is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, flower beds, and sometimes as an escape near old homesteads. It prefers rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. You might occasionally find it growing wild where seeds have scattered from nearby gardens, but it's quite rare in truly natural settings.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants develop their characteristic large, soft leaves. Plants are typically started indoors or planted out after frost danger passes.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with fragrant white trumpets opening each evening from July through August. The sweet perfume is strongest on warm, humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue until first frost kills the plant. Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing tiny seeds for next year's potential growth.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost. Only seeds remain dormant in the soil, though they rarely survive New England winters outdoors.

funFact: The flowers are specifically designed to attract night-flying sphinx moths with their evening fragrance and long trumpet shape - the moths must hover like tiny hummingbirds and unfurl their extra-long tongues to reach the nectar at the bottom of the 4-inch tubes!
confusionNotes: The evening-opening white trumpets and intense sweet fragrance make jasmine tobacco quite distinctive, though it might be confused with four o'clocks, which also open in the evening but have shorter, broader flowers and no fragrance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tobacco,' this ornamental species is grown purely for its beauty and fragrance, not for smoking. It belongs to the nightshade family along with tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, and like its relatives, all parts of the plant contain alkaloids and should not be consumed.
compareHints: Jasmine tobacco is much more delicate and ornamental than its cousin woodland tobacco, which grows much taller (up to 10 feet) with smaller white flowers. Unlike the harsh Aztec tobacco with its small yellow-green flowers, jasmine tobacco has large showy white trumpets and is grown specifically for garden beauty rather than any practical use.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woodland tobacco is much taller and more dramatic than its cousin jasmine tobacco, with longer flower tubes and larger leaves.
Aztec tobacco is much more compact and stocky than woodland tobacco, which grows 4-5 feet tall with larger white flowers.
